t: Which of the following statements regarding the 'slip' in marine insurance is correct under the Marine Insurance Act, 1963?
o: The contract is deemed concluded when the proposal is accepted by the insurer, whether or not the policy is then issued, and the slip may be referred to as evidence of the contract
The slip is the policy itself
The slip has no legal significance
The slip must be stamped before acceptance
e: Section 23 provides that the contract is concluded when the proposal is accepted (commonly by initialling the slip), and Section 89 allows reference to the slip or covering note as evidence even though the policy is issued later.

t: 'Maritime perils' as defined in the Marine Insurance Act, 1963 include all of the following EXCEPT:
o: Perils of the seas, fire, war perils and pirates
Jettison, barratry and capture
Ordinary wear and tear of the vessel
Seizures, restraints and detainments of princes and peoples
e: The Act's definition clause lists perils consequent on or incidental to navigation of the sea - perils of the seas, fire, war, pirates, thieves, captures, seizures, restraints, jettison, barratry and like perils. Ordinary wear and tear is not a fortuitous peril.

t: Which of the following best describes a 'Ro-Ro' vessel?
o: A vessel carrying liquid cargo in tanks
A vessel carrying refrigerated cargo only
A vessel on which wheeled cargo such as cars and trailers is driven on and off via ramps
A vessel carrying dry bulk cargo such as coal
e: Roll-on/Roll-off vessels have ramps allowing vehicles and trailers to be driven on board; tankers carry liquids, reefers refrigerated cargo and bulk carriers loose dry cargo.

t: Which Indian statute governs the registration, survey, safety and manning of Indian ships and is administered by the Directorate General of Shipping?
o: The Merchant Shipping Act, 1958
The Carriage by Road Act, 2007
The Multimodal Transportation of Goods Act, 1993
The Bills of Lading Act, 1856
e: The Merchant Shipping Act, 1958 is the principal legislation regulating Indian shipping, including registration, safety, crew and load lines, administered through the DG Shipping.

t: The implied warranty of legality in marine insurance requires that:
o: The vessel be registered in India
The assured be an Indian citizen
The policy be issued on stamped paper
The adventure insured be a lawful one and, so far as the assured can control it, be carried out in a lawful manner
e: Section 43 implies a warranty that the adventure is lawful and will be carried out lawfully so far as the assured can control it; a policy covering smuggling, for instance, is unenforceable.

t: Which of the following is correct concerning 'representations' made during negotiation of a marine insurance contract?
o: A representation as to a matter of fact is true if substantially correct, and a representation as to expectation or belief is true if made in good faith
Every representation must be literally true
Representations become warranties automatically
Representations are irrelevant to marine contracts
e: Section 22 distinguishes representations from warranties: a material representation of fact need only be substantially correct, and one of belief or expectation need only be made in good faith. A warranty, by contrast, requires exact compliance.

t: Which of the following is an express warranty commonly found in Indian hull policies?
o: Warranty that the vessel is seaworthy at inception
Warranty that the vessel will trade only within specified navigation limits (e.g. Institute Warranties or Indian coastal limits)
Warranty of nationality
Warranty that goods are properly packed
e: Trading or navigation limit warranties are express terms in hull policies restricting where the vessel may trade; seaworthiness is an implied warranty in voyage policies and nationality is never implied.

t: Which of the following statements about the principle of indemnity in marine cargo insurance is INCORRECT?
o: Cargo is customarily insured at CIF value plus 10% to cover anticipated profit and expenses
The agreed value in a valued policy is conclusive in the absence of fraud
The assured can recover the full insured value plus the salvage proceeds in a total loss where the goods are sold
An assured who is underinsured is his own insurer for the balance
e: Indemnity means no profit from a loss: if the assured recovers the full insured value, the insurer is entitled to the salvage/proceeds. The other statements correctly describe marine practice (agreed value, CIF+10%, underinsurance).

t: When a cargo underwriter studies the 'loss record' or 'claims experience' of a proposer over the past three to five years, he is primarily seeking to determine:
o: The proposer's tax liability
The vessel's class
Whether the proposer is a public company
The loss ratio and pattern of losses, to assess the quality of the proposer's handling, packing and carrier selection and to set an appropriate rate and deductible
e: Past claims experience is the best indicator of future performance; a high frequency of handling losses, for example, suggests weak packing or carrier selection and leads to higher rates or excesses.

t: Which of the following best explains why a cargo underwriter charges a higher rate for voyages involving transhipment?
o: Transhipment increases the freight
ICC do not cover transhipment
Transhipment is illegal under Indian law
Each additional handling and the storage at the transhipment port increase the chances of loss, and the identity of the on-carrying vessel is often unknown
e: Additional loading, discharge, storage and the uncertainty of the second vessel raise the risk; ICC continue cover during transhipment in the ordinary course of transit but underwriters rate for the added exposure.

topic: Loss Prevention, Reinsurance and Maritime Frauds
t: Under a quota share reinsurance treaty of 40%, an insurer writes a hull risk for ₹25 crore. What is the amount ceded to the reinsurer?
o: ₹15 crore
₹10 crore
₹25 crore
₹5 crore
e: ★ Key fact (repeated across the mocks of this paper). Under quota share, a fixed percentage of every risk is ceded: 40% x ₹25 crore = ₹10 crore ceded and ₹15 crore retained.

t: A hull underwriter accepts a vessel valued at ₹120 crore on a 'full form' ITC Hulls basis at a rate of 1.25% of insured value, with a deductible of ₹50 lakh. What is the annual premium (before taxes)?
o: ₹1.50 crore
₹1.20 crore
₹1.25 crore
₹15 lakh
e: Premium = ₹120 crore x 1.25% = ₹1.50 crore. The deductible affects claims, not the premium calculation.

t: Under ICC 2009, the Unseaworthiness and Unfitness Exclusion relating to a container or conveyance (Clause 5.1.2) applies only where:
o: The container is more than 5 years old
Loading is carried out prior to attachment of the insurance or by the assured or their employees and they are privy to the unfitness at the time of loading
The container is shipper-owned
The container is a reefer
e: The 2009 clauses narrowed this exclusion: unfitness of a container or conveyance is excluded only if the loading was done before attachment or by the assured/employees who were privy to the unfitness.

t: Under the Transit Clause of ICC 2009, the insurance terminates on completion of unloading at the final warehouse at destination, or on completion of unloading from the carrying vehicle at any other warehouse that the assured elects to use for:
o: Storage other than in the ordinary course of transit, or for allocation or distribution
Customs examination only
Repacking in the port area
Loading onto the ocean vessel
e: Clause 8.1 ends cover on delivery to the final warehouse or on delivery to any other warehouse chosen by the assured for storage outside the ordinary course of transit or for allocation or distribution, or 60 days after discharge, whichever first.

t: A consignment of chemicals in drums under ICC (A) was found on arrival to have lost 1.5% of its weight through normal evaporation; another 8% was lost when drums were punctured by a fork-lift during port handling. Which part of the loss is recoverable?
o: Both losses
Neither, as both are inherent to the cargo
Only the 1.5% evaporation loss
Only the 8% loss from the fork-lift accident
e: Ordinary loss in weight or volume (evaporation) is excluded by Clause 4.2, but puncturing by a fork-lift is a fortuitous external accident covered by the all-risks wording of ICC (A).

t: Under ICC 2009, the 'Avoidance of Delay' clause (Clause 18) requires that the assured shall:
o: Pay premium without delay
Avoid all transhipment
Lodge a claim within 7 days
Act with reasonable despatch in all circumstances within their control
e: Clause 18 is a condition that the assured act with reasonable despatch in circumstances within their control; unreasonable delay by the assured could prejudice cover, whereas delay beyond their control is protected by Clause 8.3.

t: The Institute War Clauses (Cargo) include a 'waterborne agreement' principle. Which of the following statements reflects it?
o: War risks on cargo are covered throughout the warehouse-to-warehouse transit
War cover is unlimited in time at a transhipment port
War risks are covered only in port
War risks on cargo attach only on loading onto the overseas vessel and cease on discharge, so that goods on land are not covered for war risks
e: Following the Waterborne Agreement, cargo war risks are confined to the period the goods are on board the vessel (with a 15-day limit at transhipment or on arrival), because land war exposure is catastrophic and uninsurable.

t: Which of the following statements about the Institute Strikes Clauses (Cargo) 1/1/2009 is INCORRECT?
o: They cover physical loss caused by strikers, locked-out workmen and persons taking part in labour disturbances, riots or civil commotions
They cover loss caused by any act of terrorism
They cover loss arising from the absence, shortage or withholding of labour of any description
They exclude loss caused by delay
e: Clause 3.7 of the Strikes Clauses expressly excludes loss, damage or expense arising from absence, shortage or withholding of labour; only physical loss caused by strikers etc. is covered.

t: Marine cargo insurance of ₹50 lakh is written at 0.08% basic rate. GST of 18% applies. What is the total amount payable by the assured?
o: ₹4,000 plus ₹720 stamp duty
e: ★ Key fact (repeated across the mocks of this paper). Premium = ₹50,00,000 x 0.08% = ₹4,000. GST at 18% = ₹720. Total = ₹4,720. Stamp duty on marine policies is a separate nominal amount and is not 18%.

t: Loss of or damage to goods in transit by air caused by an accident to the aircraft is covered under:
o: ICC (C) only
The Institute Cargo Clauses (Air), which are on all-risks terms
Hull policies
The Institute War Clauses (Cargo) only
e: The Institute Cargo Clauses (Air) provide all-risks cover (similar to ICC (A)) for goods carried by air, with exclusions for delay, inherent vice, packing and the like; war and strikes require separate Air clauses.

t: An importer insures goods under ICC (A) at CIF plus 10% and separately takes duty insurance for ₹6 lakh. The goods arrive 20% damaged by an insured peril and the importer has to pay full customs duty. The duty insurer pays:
o: ₹6 lakh
₹1.2 lakh, being the same percentage of depreciation as under the cargo policy
Nil, because duty insurance pays only on total loss
₹3 lakh
e: Duty insurance follows the cargo claim: the duty insurer pays the same proportion of the duty sum insured as the depreciation admitted under the cargo policy, i.e. 20% of ₹6 lakh = ₹1.2 lakh.

t: Which of the following statements about an Open Cover is INCORRECT?
o: It is an unstamped agreement under which stamped certificates or policies are issued for each declaration
It specifies the rates, conditions, limit per bottom and location limit in advance
It is itself a stamped policy on which a claim can be made without any declaration
It requires the assured to declare all shipments within its scope
e: An open cover is not a policy; a claim is made on the stamped certificate or specific policy issued against the declaration. The other statements correctly describe an open cover.

t: Under an Open Policy in India, if a despatch is accidentally omitted from declaration and a loss occurs, the usual position is:
o: The claim is automatically rejected
The policy becomes void
The claim is paid at 50%
If the omission was inadvertent and in good faith, the assured may declare it after the event and the insurer generally honours the claim, subject to the policy's sum insured not being exhausted
e: Open policies commonly contain a provision allowing genuine, inadvertent omissions to be rectified after loss, because the assured is bound to declare all despatches and the insurer receives premium for them.

t: Which cover is appropriate for a shipowner's or charterer's loss of freight when the vessel is unable to earn it because of an insured casualty?
o: Freight insurance (e.g. Institute Time Clauses - Freight)
Duty insurance
ICC (A)
Seller's interest cover
e: Freight insurance protects the shipowner's or charterer's interest in freight at risk; it is a distinct marine interest from hull and cargo.

t: A 'Marine Cum Erection' or 'Marine Cum Storage' extension in Indian practice links the marine cargo policy with:
o: The project's erection/storage cover so that there is continuity between transit and storage/erection at site
The hull policy of the carrying vessel
The buyer's bank guarantee
The customs duty bond
e: For project cargo, marine transit cover is often combined with storage-cum-erection cover so that no gap arises between delivery at site and the erection policy; it is usually packaged with an EAR/CAR policy.

t: Which of the following is correct about 'Contingency' insurance taken by a seller on FOB terms?
o: It replaces the buyer's obligation to insure
It is disclosed to the buyer and assigned to him
It responds only if the buyer fails to pay for goods lost or damaged in transit and the seller cannot recover under the buyer's insurance
It covers war risks on land
e: Seller's contingency insurance is a non-disclosed, non-assignable cover for the seller's exposure where the buyer defaults after a transit loss, and the buyer's insurance (if any) does not inure to the seller.

t: A hull policy under ITC Hulls 83 carries a deductible of ₹25 lakh. The vessel sustained particular average damage of ₹90 lakh in one accident. What is the insurer's liability?
o: ₹90 lakh
₹65 lakh
₹25 lakh
₹1.15 crore
e: ★ Key fact (repeated across the mocks of this paper). The deductible of ₹25 lakh is deducted from the aggregate of all claims arising from each separate accident: ₹90 lakh - ₹25 lakh = ₹65 lakh. The deductible does not apply to a total or constructive total loss.

t: Which of the following statements regarding the 'Plimsoll line' or load line is correct?
o: It indicates the vessel's maximum speed
It marks the maximum depth to which a vessel may be legally loaded in different zones and seasons, under the International Load Line Convention
It shows the location of the engine room
It is the line of ownership
e: The load line marks on the hull show the permissible draught in tropical, summer, winter and fresh-water conditions; loading beyond it renders the vessel unseaworthy and breaches international and Indian law.

t: Under ITC Hulls 83, earthquake and volcanic eruption are:
o: Covered under Clause 6.1
Excluded
Covered only if the vessel is in port
Covered under the war clauses
e: Clause 6.1.6 covers earthquake, volcanic eruption or lightning as a peril of the hull policy, without any due diligence proviso.

t: The 'New for Old' clause (Clause 14) of ITC Hulls 83 provides that:
o: Claims are payable without deduction new for old
Claims are reduced by one-third for new materials replacing old
Only new vessels are insurable
Old vessels are paid at scrap value
e: Under ITC Hulls, repairs are paid without any 'new for old' deduction, departing from the old practice of deducting one-third for betterment.

t: A hull insured under ITC Hulls 83 was damaged when the vessel grounded because the charts in use were outdated and the owners had ignored repeated class recommendations to update navigational equipment. Which of the following is the most likely outcome?
o: Fully covered, as grounding is a peril of the seas regardless of cause
Covered only under war risks
Not covered because grounding is excluded

Grounding is a Clause 6.1 peril so the claim is in principle recoverable, but underwriters may raise unseaworthiness with privity of the assured (Section 41(5)) or breach of the class warranty if class had been withdrawn
e: Perils of the seas in Clause 6.1 are not subject to the due diligence proviso, but the Act's privity rule on unseaworthiness in time policies and the classification clause can still defeat a claim where the owner knowingly sent the ship to sea unseaworthy.

t: Under ITC Hulls 83, 'violent theft by persons from outside the vessel' is covered, whereas theft by the crew is:
o: Also covered under Clause 6.1
Not covered as a peril, unless it amounts to barratry of the master, officers or crew under Clause 6.2
Covered under the war clauses
Covered only on a voyage policy
e: Clause 6.1.3 is limited to violent theft from outside the vessel; dishonesty of the crew is only covered where it constitutes barratry (a wilful wrongful act to the prejudice of the owner), subject to the due diligence proviso.

t: Under the 3/4ths Collision Liability clause, the insurer also pays 3/4ths of the legal costs incurred by the assured in contesting liability or taking proceedings to limit liability, provided:
o: The assured pays the full costs first
The costs are incurred with the prior written consent of the underwriters
The other vessel is Indian
The collision occurred in port
e: Clause 8.3 extends to 3/4ths of legal costs incurred with underwriters' prior written consent; this is in addition to the 3/4ths of liability for damages.

t: Which of the following is NOT a type of return of premium under ITC Hulls 83?
o: Return for cancellation by agreement
Return for lay-up of 30 consecutive days in an approved port or area
Return for 'no claims' at the end of the policy
Pro rata net return if the vessel is laid up under repair for a qualifying period
e: Clause 22 provides returns for cancellation by agreement and for lay-up periods of 30 consecutive days (at differing rates for 'under repair' and 'not under repair'). There is no no-claims return under the standard clauses.

t: Under ITC Hulls 83, the vessel is insured for ₹45 crore and an Increased Value (Disbursements) policy is also taken. Under the Disbursements Warranty, the maximum permissible increased value insurance is:
o: ₹4.5 crore
₹11.25 crore
₹22.5 crore
₹45 crore
e: The Disbursements Warranty limits disbursements and increased value insurance to 25% of the hull value: 25% x ₹45 crore = ₹11.25 crore.

t: Which of the following liabilities of a shipowner is typically covered by a P&I Club rather than by the hull policy under ITC Hulls 83?
o: Three-fourths of collision liability for damage to another vessel
Particular average damage to the insured vessel
Liability for pollution, wreck removal, cargo claims and loss of life or injury to crew
Constructive total loss of the vessel
e: The hull policy covers physical damage and 3/4ths collision liability; liabilities excluded by Clause 8.4 (pollution, wreck removal, cargo on the insured vessel, personal injury) and the remaining 1/4th collision are P&I risks.

t: The principle that allows an insurer who has paid a claim to step into the insured's shoes and recover from a liable third party is:
o: Contribution
Subrogation
Indemnity
Proximate cause
e: ★ Core fact (asked across III papers). Subrogation is a corollary of indemnity; it does not apply to life or personal accident (benefit) policies.

t: Under the Marine Insurance Act, 1963, where goods reach their destination in specie but by reason of obliteration of marks they are incapable of identification, the loss is:
o: An actual total loss
A constructive total loss
A partial loss
Not a loss at all
e: Section 56(5) provides that where goods arrive in specie but cannot be identified because the marks are obliterated, the loss, if any, is partial and not total.

t: Which of the following is an essential feature of 'salvage charges' as defined in Section 65 of the Marine Insurance Act, 1963?
o: They are payable to the assured's own employees for saving the cargo
They are charges recoverable under maritime law by a salvor independently of contract
They are always treated as general average
They are paid by the carrier only
e: Salvage charges are payable to a volunteer salvor under maritime law independently of contract; expenses incurred by the assured's own agents are particular charges or GA, not salvage charges.

t: A cargo policy carries an excess (deductible) of 1% of the insured value of ₹60 lakh. The assessed loss is ₹2,40,000. The amount payable is:
o: Nil
e: Deductible = 1% of ₹60 lakh = ₹60,000. Under a deductible only the amount in excess is paid: ₹2,40,000 - ₹60,000 = ₹1,80,000. Under a franchise the full amount would have been payable.

t: In a general average adjustment, the 'contributory value' of cargo is normally based on:
o: The insured value plus 10%
The CIF value doubled
The freight paid
The value at the time and place of discharge, ascertained from the commercial invoice, less any loss that is not made good in GA, plus any amount made good as GA
e: Under York-Antwerp Rule XVII, cargo contributes on its value at discharge ascertained from the commercial invoice (or shipped value), deducting loss or damage not made good, and adding the amount made good in general average.

t: A consignment under ICC (A) was damaged by sea water and the consignee refused to accept delivery. The surveyor found that part of the goods could be reconditioned at a cost of ₹2 lakh, which would restore them to a value of ₹9 lakh against a sound value of ₹10 lakh; otherwise they would fetch only ₹4 lakh. The most appropriate settlement basis is:
o: Pay the reconditioning cost of ₹2 lakh plus the residual depreciation of 10%, since this minimises the loss
Pay the full insured value as a total loss
Reject the claim because the consignee refused delivery
Pay only ₹4 lakh
e: The duty to minimise the loss (Clause 16) and the measure of indemnity favour reconditioning where it is economical: reconditioning cost plus the remaining depreciation produces a much smaller claim than a salvage loss or total loss.

t: Under the Carriage by Road Act, 2007 and the rules thereunder, the liability of a common carrier for loss of goods, where no higher value has been declared and extra charge paid, is limited to:
o: Ten times the freight paid
The full invoice value
₹1 lakh per consignment
666.67 SDR per package
e: The Carriage by Road Rules, 2011 limit the common carrier's liability to ten times the freight unless the consignor declares a higher value and pays the applicable additional charge.

t: A 'Letter of Subrogation' signed by the assured at the time of claim settlement:
o: Transfers ownership of the goods to the insurer
Is required only for hull claims
Waives the insurer's rights against the carrier
Confirms the insurer's right to pursue recovery against third parties in the assured's name and the assured's undertaking to cooperate
e: Although subrogation arises by law on payment, the letter of subrogation (with a receipt) documents the right, records the assured's undertaking to assist and allows the insurer to sue in the assured's name.

t: In a life insurance contract, insurable interest must exist:
o: At the time of the claim only
At inception of the policy
Both at inception and at claim
At renewal each year
e: ★ Core fact (asked across III papers). Life: at inception only. Marine: at the time of loss. Fire and motor: at both inception and loss.

t: A cargo insurer is contemplating a recovery suit against a shipping line under a bill of lading subject to the Hague-Visby Rules. The goods were delivered damaged on 10 March 2025 and no extension of time was obtained. The last date for filing suit is:
o: 10 June 2025
10 September 2025
10 March 2026
10 March 2027
e: Under Article III rule 6 of the Hague-Visby Rules the carrier is discharged from all liability unless suit is brought within one year of delivery; hence 10 March 2026 (unless the parties agree an extension).

topic: Role of Banker in Marine Insurance
t: 'Hypothecation' of goods in transit by a bank differs from 'pledge' in that under hypothecation:
o: The borrower retains possession of the goods and the bank has only a charge over them
The bank takes physical possession of the goods
The goods are sold immediately
The insurer becomes the owner
e: In a pledge the bank holds possession (e.g. via the bill of lading); under hypothecation the goods remain with the borrower subject to the bank's charge, which is why banks insist on insurance with a bank clause.

topic: Role of Banker in Marine Insurance
t: Under UCP 600 Article 28, the currency of the insurance document must be:
o: Indian Rupees always
The currency of the credit
US Dollars always
Any currency chosen by the insurer
e: The insurance document must be expressed in the same currency as the credit so that the bank's security is not exposed to exchange risk.

topic: Loss Prevention, Reinsurance and Maritime Frauds
t: Which of the following is a 'documentary fraud' in maritime trade?
o: A vessel sinking in a storm
Delay in arrival of the vessel
Jettison of cargo during a storm
Presentation of forged or falsified bills of lading or other shipping documents under a letter of credit for goods that were never shipped or were of inferior quality
e: Documentary fraud exploits the fact that banks deal in documents, not goods; forged bills of lading, invoices or insurance certificates are used to obtain payment under a credit.

topic: Loss Prevention, Reinsurance and Maritime Frauds
t: Facultative reinsurance differs from treaty reinsurance in that under facultative reinsurance:
o: The reinsurer must accept every risk automatically
It covers only total losses
It is used only for cargo
Each risk is offered and accepted individually, giving the reinsurer the option to decline
e: Facultative reinsurance is placed risk by risk, with the reinsurer free to accept or reject; treaties bind the reinsurer to accept all risks falling within the agreed scope.
